q-ph-meaning.label: Meaning of a phrasal verb
q-ph-meaning.summary: A phrasal verb in a sentence; pick what it means there.

q-ph-fit.label: The phrasal verb that fits
q-ph-fit.summary: A sentence with a blank; pick the phrasal verb whose meaning the sentence needs.

rules.text: The particle carries the meaning, so one verb makes many different phrasal verbs: put off (postpone), put up with (tolerate), put down (write, or humiliate), put out (extinguish). Read the particle, not just the verb.
rules.ok: The match was put off because of rain (postponed).
rules.bad: The match was put off because of rain (extinguished).

rules.text: A phrasal verb almost never means its literal picture. If one option simply describes the physical action of the verb and the particle, it is the bait.
rules.ok: He turned down the offer (refused it).
rules.bad: He turned down the offer (rotated it downwards).

rules.text: For a blank, work out what the sentence needs in plain words first (stop, tolerate, discover, postpone), and only then look for the phrasal verb that says it. Check that the particle and the object fit: you put up WITH a person, you look INTO a matter.
rules.ok: The police will look into the complaint (investigate it).
rules.bad: The police will look after the complaint (take care of it).

q-ph-meaning.cue: A sentence with a phrasal verb in inverted commas or highlighted, and four meanings as options.
q-ph-meaning.standard: Read the whole sentence, decide from the situation what the speaker must mean, then match the option.
q-ph-meaning.fast: Translate the phrasal verb into one plain word in your head, then look for that word among the options.
q-ph-meaning.eliminate: Drop the literal reading at once, then drop meanings that belong to the same verb with a different particle.
traps: The literal picture of the words.
The meaning of the same verb with another particle (put off / put up with).
Two options that are close in sense: the sentence decides which.

q-ph-fit.cue: A sentence with a blank and four phrasal verbs as options.
q-ph-fit.standard: Say what the sentence needs in one plain word, then test each option in the blank.
q-ph-fit.fast: Check the particle against the object: 'into' a matter, 'with' a person, 'for' a thing you want.
q-ph-fit.eliminate: Remove options whose particle cannot take that object at all.
traps: Two options from the same verb (look into, look after, look for).
A phrasal verb that fits the grammar but not the situation.

pyqs.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
They ______ the table beautifully for their guests.
options: laid in
laid out
laid by
laid on
pyqs.why: The sentence needs 'arranged attractively', which is what 'lay out' means: they laid out the table.

a.note: 'Laid in' means to store up a supply of something, not to arrange a table.

c.note: 'Laid by' means to set something aside for later use, not to arrange a table.

d.note: 'Laid on' means to arrange or provide a service or event, which is close but is not the phrase used for arranging a table setting itself.

d.note: That is what 'go through' means, not 'put off'.

'turn up'
options: To prove to be the case in the end
To abolish something
To postpone something to a later time
To arrive or appear, often unexpectedly
practice.why: 'turn up' means: to arrive or appear, often unexpectedly.

a.note: That is what 'turn out' means, not 'turn up'. The verb is the same, so only the particle tells them apart.

b.note: That is what 'do away with' means, not 'turn up'.

c.note: That is what 'put off' means, not 'turn up'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the phrasal verb in the sentence.
The rumour [[turned out]] to be false.
'turn out'
options: To prove to be the case in the end
To refuse an offer or a request
To cancel something that was planned
To raise a child
practice.why: 'turn out' means: to prove to be the case in the end.

b.note: That is what 'turn down' means, not 'turn out'. The verb is the same, so only the particle tells them apart.

c.note: That is what 'call off' means, not 'turn out'.

d.note: That is what 'bring up' means, not 'turn out'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the phrasal verb in the sentence.
The state [[did away with]] the old levy.
'do away with'
options: To confirm that something is true
To abolish something
To extinguish a fire or a light
To begin suddenly, said of something unwelcome such as a war or a disease
practice.why: 'do away with' means: to abolish something.

a.note: That is what 'bear out' means, not 'do away with'.

c.note: That is what 'put out' means, not 'do away with'.

d.note: That is what 'break out' means, not 'do away with'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the phrasal verb in the sentence.
His colleagues [[stood by]] him through the inquiry.
'stand by'
options: To perform or complete a task or an order
To meet or find something by chance
To support someone in a difficulty
To stop doing something one has been doing regularly
practice.why: 'stand by' means: to support someone in a difficulty.

a.note: That is what 'carry out' means, not 'stand by'.

b.note: That is what 'come across' means, not 'stand by'.

d.note: That is what 'give up' means, not 'stand by'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the phrasal verb in the sentence.
The records [[bear out]] his account.
'bear out'
options: To recover from an illness or an unhappy event
To investigate a matter
To compensate for something lost or missed
To confirm that something is true
practice.why: 'bear out' means: to confirm that something is true.

a.note: That is what 'get over' means, not 'bear out'.

b.note: That is what 'look into' means, not 'bear out'.

c.note: That is what 'make up for' means, not 'bear out'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the phrasal verb in the sentence.
He promised to come and then let [[us down]].
'let down'
options: To disappoint someone by failing them
To regard someone as inferior
To meet someone unexpectedly
To arrive or appear, often unexpectedly
practice.why: 'let down' means: to disappoint someone by failing them.

b.note: That is what 'look down on' means, not 'let down'.

c.note: That is what 'run into' means, not 'let down'.

d.note: That is what 'turn up' means, not 'let down'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the phrasal verb in the sentence.
An accident [[held up]] the traffic for an hour.
'hold up'
options: To assume control of something
To delay something or someone
To confirm that something is true
To write something on paper
practice.why: 'hold up' means: to delay something or someone.

a.note: That is what 'take over' means, not 'hold up'.

c.note: That is what 'bear out' means, not 'hold up'.

d.note: That is what 'put down' means, not 'hold up'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the phrasal verb in the sentence.
If the loan is refused we can [[fall back on]] our savings.
'fall back on'
options: To postpone something to a later time
To continue doing something
To use something as a last resort when other plans fail
To think of an idea or a plan
practice.why: 'fall back on' means: to use something as a last resort when other plans fail.

a.note: That is what 'put off' means, not 'fall back on'.

b.note: That is what 'carry on' means, not 'fall back on'.

d.note: That is what 'come up with' means, not 'fall back on'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the phrasal verb in the sentence.
The staff [[lay out]] fresh linen on every bed each morning.
'lay out'
options: To raise a child
To remove or throw away something unwanted
To take care of a person or a thing
To arrange or spread something out neatly and attractively
practice.why: 'lay out' means: to arrange or spread something out neatly and attractively.

a.note: That is what 'bring up' means, not 'lay out'.

b.note: That is what 'get rid of' means, not 'lay out'.

c.note: That is what 'look after' means, not 'lay out'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The department has promised to ___ the complaint within a month.
options: look after
look into
look for
look up to
practice.why: The sentence needs 'investigate', which is what 'look into' means.

a.note: 'Look after' means to take care of something, and a complaint is not cared for but examined.

c.note: 'Look for' means to search for a thing that is missing; the complaint is already in hand.

d.note: 'Look up to' means to respect a person and cannot take a complaint as its object.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
She had to ___ a great deal of rudeness from the callers.
options: put up with
put off
put out
put down
practice.why: The sentence needs 'tolerate', which is what 'put up with' means.

b.note: 'Put off' means to postpone, and rudeness is not postponed.

c.note: 'Put out' means to extinguish a fire or a light.

d.note: 'Put down' means to write something on paper.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The records ___ his account of the meeting.
options: bear out
break out
turn out
make out
practice.why: The sentence needs 'confirm', which is what 'bear out' means.

b.note: 'Break out' means to begin suddenly, said of a war or a disease.

c.note: 'Turn out' means to prove to be the case, but it does not take an object in this way: an account turns out to be true, it is not turned out by records.

d.note: 'Make out' means to manage to see or understand something with difficulty.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
If the bank refuses the loan, we can ___ our savings.
options: fall back on
give in to
do away with
run out of
practice.why: The sentence needs 'use as a last resort', which is what 'fall back on' means.

b.note: 'Give in to' means to stop resisting something, which savings are not.

c.note: 'Do away with' means to abolish, which would mean getting rid of the savings rather than using them.

d.note: 'Run out of' means to exhaust a supply, which is the opposite of having savings to rely on.
